correctness.rationale: A uniformly contractive backward Euler recursion admits a stationary conditional Gaussian representation. Its mixing variance lies between deterministic-step fixed-point variances. A first-long-step geometric decomposition proves the sharp endpoint small-ball exponent; Mills bounds and Laplace estimates rigorously transfer this to the two-sided tail law. Two rational examples match their mean step and stationary squared error, but have distinct logarithmic tail rates. The included verification code passed 50,315 finite diagnostic assertions; it is not the proof of the infinite statements.

originality.rationale: The accepted theorem is the exact two-sided Gaussian-extreme-tail correction under two-atom random backward Euler steps and a matched-moment, exponentially separated risk witness. Broad BEM invariant-measure papers and previously recorded general stochastic-theta moments do not state these tail conclusions. A bounded Bernoulli affine variance perpetuity and Gaussian tail transfer are individually classical ingredients; publication priority against specialized combinations remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: A general published theorem for endpoint tails of affine perpetuities composed with Gaussian scale mixtures might implicitly subsume the derived asymptotic; bibliographic completeness cannot be guaranteed.
The result measures stationarity per update rather than uniformly in physical time; this distinction matters when interpreting the matched-mean witness.
The two-sided power law is Θ rather than an exact constant; arithmetic small-ball oscillations may persist.

value.rationale: This gives a natural, reproducible extreme-event reliability benchmark for random-step numerical sampling: identical mean time step and identical stationary squared error fail to control exponentially different rare-event tails. The polynomial correction quantitatively isolates the probability of runs of the shortest step. This is a distributional phenomenon not captured by variance or kurtosis classification alone.
